newsitem.title: THAILAND: Moody's dumps bad news on battered Thai markets.
newsitem.headline: Moody's dumps bad news on battered Thai markets.

text.p: Thailand's battered financial markets will be set back for several more months, especially after Friday's news that ratings agency Moody's may cut the nation's long-term debt ratings, analysts said.

Moody's Investors Service said it had placed Thailand's A2 long-term foreign debt rating under review for a possible downgrade. It also said it may cut the A2 long-term foreign currency bond and deposit ratings for five major Thai banks.

The news sent the stock market, now near 56-month lows, and the baht reeling. It also drew a sharp response from the central Bank of Thailand, which disagreed with the Moody's view and demanded reasons for the agency's action.
At the lunch break on Friday, the Thai stock index was down a hefty 4.53 percent or 31.64 points at 666.42, after closing on Thursday at a 56-month low.
"We would like to see the reasons why they did this, because we think the situation is improving and will improve further over time," a central bank spokeswoman told Reuters.
"The bank is doing all it can at the moment through the economy but these things take time to work out. You can't expect them to happen overnight," Duangmanee Vongpratit said.
Analysts said any Moody's ratings downgrade would raise the cost of borrowing funds for Thailand and the five banks.
But Siam Commercial Bank Plc, one of the five banks named for a possible ratings cut by Moody's, said any downgrade would not have a major effect on bank borrowing costs.

"There will be some impact on the bank's cost of funds, but not significantly so. The bank's funding from offshore resources represented only 10 percent of total funding," senior vice-president PrakitPadipasen told reporters.
The other banks named by Moody's are Bangkok Bank, the Export-Import Bank of Thailand, Industrial Finance Corp of Thailand, and Thai Farmers Bank.

"The possible downgrade coming at this time won't help one bit. There is a crisis of confidence affecting Thailand and the next three to six months will be crucial," said the head of an American investment bank who declined to be identified.

The sliding baht has been hammered by devaluation rumours and speculative attacks by offshore players. It has plummeted against the surging dollar and was trading at a weak 26.100-26.150 in the early afternoon on Friday.
To counter the attacks on the baht, the central bank has allowed domestic interest rates to soar, which in turn has led to a liquidity squeeze in the local money market.
Analysts said the high rates had filled the tumbling stock market with rumours that some listed financial institutions may be hit by the current liquidity crunch, and sentiment had been badly dented.
A slow economy, deep spending cuts for fiscal 1996/97 (Sept-Oct) and a perception that the Thai government had not acted firmly had cast a pall over Thailand, they added.

"People don't believe this government has the stamina or guts to fight baht speculation. The Bank of Thailand is playing a gentleman's game against speculators, supporting the baht while losing valuable foreign reserves," said the investment bank head.

"At the moment, the sentiment of the Thai financial market is particulary weak," said Desmond Supple, senior economist at the Singapore-based research house, I.D.E.A. "If we throw the issue of a potential downgrade into the melting pot, then it could be disastrous."
Analysts said the Bank of Thailand needed to act more firmly to curb foreign borrowing which was a major factor behind Moody's possible downgrade.
